unsupervised-and-semi-supervised-learnin.text: Most real datasets arrive without labels, or with far fewer labels than you need. That constraint splits the work three ways. You can look for structure directly, grouping records that behave alike. You can look for a shorter description of each record, compressing hundreds of raw columns into a handful of meaningful numbers. Or you can accept that a few labels exist and stretch them as far as possible, borrowing signal from unlabelled data or from a model someone else already trained. Clustering, dimensionality reduction, and learning with limited labels are those three answers, and in practice a project uses more than one.
unsupervised-and-semi-supervised-learnin.deep_text:
The organising question here is what you do when the labels are missing, scarce, or expensive. Clustering comes first because it is the most direct response: leave the data as it is, define a notion of similarity, and let the algorithm propose groups. It teaches the habit that unsupervised results are proposals to be validated, not answers with an accuracy score attached. Dimensionality reduction and representation comes second because it changes the data rather than partitioning it. Instead of asking which records belong together, it asks which coordinates are worth keeping, and it produces a new feature space that downstream models, including clustering itself, work better in. That dependency is why the order matters: clustering in a raw thousand-column space often fails for reasons the representation section explains. Learning with limited labels comes third because it presumes both of the earlier tools. Detecting anomalies means having a model of what normal looks like. Self-supervised pretraining and transfer learning are, in effect, ways of manufacturing a representation without paying for annotation. Active learning closes the loop by deciding which handful of records is worth sending to a human annotator. Read in that order, each part supplies something the next one leans on, and the section as a whole becomes a toolkit for the common situation where you have plenty of data and very little of it labelled.

One warning applies across all three parts, and it is why this section demands more judgement than supervised learning does. There is no held-out score to appeal to. A supervised model is right or wrong against labels you already trust, and the argument about whether it works can be settled with a number. Here, nothing tells you the grouping is the correct grouping. Every method in this section will return a confident-looking answer on data with no structure whatsoever, and none of them will warn you. Validation therefore comes from outside the algorithm: stability across resampled subsets and random seeds, agreement between methods with genuinely different assumptions, and whether the output survives contact with someone who knows the domain.

clustering.text: Grouping records by similarity sounds like one task, but there is no single definition of a group, and that is why several algorithms exist rather than one. A group can mean points near a common centre, or points that merge early as you build a tree, or a connected region where points are packed densely, or a probability distribution that the point most likely came from. Each definition makes different assumptions about shape, size, and whether every point must belong somewhere. Picking an algorithm is really picking which of those assumptions matches your data.
clustering.deep_text:
The children here divide along two axes: what counts as a cluster, and how the algorithm commits points to one. K-means starts the sequence because it is the simplest commitment — a cluster is whatever is closest to a centre, and the algorithm alternates between assigning points and moving centres. Choosing K follows immediately, because k-means and several of its relatives will happily return any number of clusters you ask for, so the question of how many is a separate skill with its own diagnostics; it belongs to that node rather than being re-derived inside each algorithm. Hierarchical clustering then relaxes the requirement to commit to a number at all, producing a whole nested family of solutions you can cut at any level. DBSCAN relaxes the assumption that clusters are blobs around a centre, defining them instead by density and, importantly, allowing points to belong to nothing. Gaussian mixtures relax the assumption of hard membership, giving each point a probability of belonging to each component. The arc runs from most rigid to most flexible, and flexibility costs you either interpretability or compute. A practical workflow often runs two of them and compares: agreement between methods with different assumptions is far stronger evidence that the structure is real than any single run.

Worth knowing before you start: all five share a dependence on how you measure similarity, and that choice is usually more consequential than which of the five you pick. Change the distance function or the scaling of your columns and the same algorithm returns different clusters — so if two of these methods disagree, the first thing to examine is the feature space rather than the algorithms. Both concerns are settled elsewhere, in the sections on feature scaling and on representation, and they are worth settling before reaching for anything here.

k-means-and-centroid-assignment.text: K-means represents each cluster by a single point, its centroid, and then runs a two-step loop until nothing changes. Assign every data point to the nearest centroid. Recompute each centroid as the mean of the points now assigned to it. Repeat. Each pass can only lower the total squared distance from points to their centroids, so the loop always terminates, though at a local minimum that depends on where the centroids started. That is the whole algorithm: alternate between fixing the assignments and fixing the centres, and the geometry does the rest.
k-means-and-centroid-assignment.deep_text:
Work through a tiny case. Six one-dimensional customers with monthly spend 2, 3, 4, 20, 21, 23, and two centroids initialised badly at 2 and 3. First assignment: point 2 goes to centroid 2; everything else is closer to 3. Recompute: the first centroid stays at 2, the second becomes the mean of 3, 4, 20, 21, 23, which is 14.2. Second assignment: 2, 3, and 4 are now closer to 2 than to 14.2, so they move over; 20, 21, 23 stay. Recompute: centroids become 3 and 21.33. Third pass changes no assignment, so it stops. Note how one bad initialisation cost two extra iterations, and how a different start could have split the low group in half and never recovered. This is why implementations run several restarts with spread-out seeds and keep the best result by total squared distance.

The most common misconception is that k-means finds the globally best partition. It does not, and it cannot; the objective it minimises has many local minima, and the loop only guarantees it will not get worse. A second, subtler error is treating the centroid as a real member of the data. It is an average, and on categorical or one-hot features the average is often a point no customer could ever be — 0.4 of a subscription tier means nothing. Because distance to a mean is the only currency, the assumptions are strong: clusters end up roughly spherical, roughly equal in size, and every point is forced into one, so a single extreme outlier drags a centroid toward it and distorts the boundary.

Reach for k-means when the features are continuous, comparably scaled — standardise first, or the column measured in rupees will dominate the one measured in years — and you expect compact, similarly sized groups. It scales to millions of rows and is easy to explain to a stakeholder, which matters more than it should. Avoid it when clusters are elongated or nested, when sizes differ by orders of magnitude, or when you need some points to be labelled as belonging nowhere at all.

interview.question: Why does k-means give you a different answer on different runs, and what do you do about it?
interview.answer: The loop converges to a local minimum of within-cluster squared distance, and which minimum you land in depends entirely on the initial centroids. Two random starts can produce genuinely different partitions of the same data. The standard mitigation is many restarts with a spread-out initialisation scheme and keeping the run with the lowest objective, plus fixing a seed so results are reproducible when you report them.

interview.question: When would you not reach for k-means even though it is the obvious first choice?
interview.answer: When the geometry violates its assumptions. Elongated or crescent-shaped groups, clusters whose sizes differ by orders of magnitude, or data with real outliers that should not belong to any group will all produce misleading centroids. Categorical-heavy data is another case, since the mean of one-hot columns is not an interpretable point.

interview.question: Someone hands you unscaled features and a k-means result. What is your first concern?
interview.answer: That the clustering is really just a partition on whichever feature has the largest numeric range. Distance to a centroid weights every column equally in raw units, so annual income in the tens of thousands will swamp age in the tens. I would standardise or otherwise put features on comparable scales and rerun before believing anything about the groups.

choosing-k-elbow-and-silhouette.text: Nothing in a clustering algorithm tells you how many clusters the data actually has, so the number becomes a modelling decision you have to justify. Two diagnostics dominate. The elbow method plots how much within-cluster spread remains as you increase the number of clusters and looks for the bend where extra clusters stop buying much. Silhouette scores each point by comparing how close it sits to its own cluster versus the nearest rival cluster, giving a value you can average. They often disagree, and where they disagree, the domain usually decides.
choosing-k-elbow-and-silhouette.deep_text:
Concretely, suppose you cluster 5,000 users and record total within-cluster sum of squares for each candidate count: 48,000 at two, 26,000 at three, 19,000 at four, 17,500 at five, 16,600 at six. The drops are 22,000, then 7,000, then 1,500, then 900. The curve bends hard between three and four, and after four you are paying a whole extra cluster for a rounding error. That bend is the elbow. Now compute silhouettes: each point's score is the gap between its average distance to points in the nearest other cluster and its average distance to its own cluster, divided by whichever is larger. Scores near one mean the point sits comfortably inside its group; near zero means it sits on a boundary; negative means it is closer to a different cluster than its own. If four clusters average 0.42 and three average 0.51, silhouette is arguing for three while the elbow leans four, and you now have a real question to answer rather than a number to accept.

The misconception worth killing is that these are objective tests with a pass mark. They are not. Within-cluster spread decreases monotonically as you add clusters — at one cluster per point it hits zero — so the metric alone always prefers more, and the elbow is a subjective reading of a curve that is frequently smooth with no visible bend at all. Silhouette has its own bias: it rewards compact, well-separated, roughly spherical groups, so on genuinely elongated or density-defined structure it will score the correct answer poorly. Neither metric knows anything about what the clusters mean.

The decision rule in practice is to treat both curves as a shortlist generator, not a decider. Take the two or three candidate values they suggest, inspect the resulting clusters directly — sizes, top distinguishing features, a handful of example records — and pick the one a domain expert can name. A five-cluster solution where one cluster holds eleven users is worse than a three-cluster solution someone can act on. Also check stability: refit on bootstrap resamples and see whether the same number keeps winning. A choice that flips between four and seven depending on which 80% of the data you use is telling you the structure is weak, which is itself the most useful finding you will get that day.

interview.question: Why can't you just pick the number of clusters that minimises within-cluster sum of squares?
interview.answer: Because that quantity decreases monotonically with more clusters and reaches zero when every point is its own cluster. The metric has no penalty for complexity, so optimising it directly always drives you to the degenerate solution. That is exactly why you look for a bend in the curve rather than its minimum.

interview.question: The elbow and silhouette disagree. How do you resolve it?
interview.answer: I treat both as producing a shortlist rather than a verdict, then inspect the actual clusters at each candidate value — sizes, distinguishing features, sample records. The tiebreaker is whether a domain expert can name the groups and act differently on them. I would also check stability across resamples, since a number that flips run to run indicates the structure is weak regardless of which metric won.

interview.question: When is silhouette a misleading metric?
interview.answer: When the true clusters are not compact and roughly spherical. Silhouette is built on average distances to own versus nearest cluster, so elongated, nested, or density-defined shapes score badly even when the partition is correct. It also degrades in very high dimensions where distances concentrate and every point looks equidistant from everything.

hierarchical-clustering.text: Rather than committing to a number of groups, hierarchical clustering builds a whole nested family of them. The agglomerative version starts with every point as its own cluster, repeatedly merges the two closest clusters, and stops when one cluster remains. Recording the order and the distance of each merge gives you a dendrogram, a tree whose height shows how dissimilar the things being joined were. Cutting that tree at any height yields a partition, so you get every possible number of clusters from one run, and the nesting itself is often the interesting result.
hierarchical-clustering.deep_text:
The choice that decides everything is linkage: once two clusters contain several points each, what does the distance between them mean? Single linkage uses the closest pair, complete linkage the farthest pair, average linkage the mean over all cross-pairs, and Ward's method merges the pair that increases total within-cluster variance least. Take five products with pairwise distances where A and B sit 0.1 apart, C and D sit 0.15 apart, and E sits 0.6 from everything. Merge A with B at height 0.1, then C with D at 0.15. Now, joining the AB and CD groups costs 0.3 under single linkage if the nearest cross-pair is 0.3, but 0.55 under complete linkage if the farthest is 0.55. Those two dendrograms have different shapes and, cut at the same height, different cluster counts. Single linkage is prone to chaining — a thin bridge of intermediate points welds two obviously distinct groups together — while complete linkage forces compact clusters and will split an elongated one. Ward's tends to give the most balanced trees on continuous data and is the common default.

The misconception to correct is that the dendrogram reveals a true hierarchy in the data. It does not. The algorithm is greedy and always produces a tree, even on uniform random noise, and every merge is final — a point placed early can never be moved, so an early mistake propagates all the way to the root. A tall, tidy-looking dendrogram from random data is a standard demonstration of this. Treat the tree as one summary among several, not a discovered taxonomy.

Reach for it when the nesting is genuinely meaningful — biological taxonomies, document topic trees, organisational structures — or when you want to see the structure at every granularity before committing. It is also the natural fit when all you have is a distance matrix and no coordinates, since it never needs to compute a mean. The hard limit is cost: naive implementations are quadratic in memory and worse in time, so tens of thousands of points is roughly the practical ceiling without approximation. Above that, cluster a sample, or use a method that does not need all pairwise distances.

interview.question: How does linkage choice change your results, and which would you default to?
interview.answer: Linkage defines the distance between two multi-point clusters, and it changes both the shape of the tree and the partition you get at any cut height. Single linkage chains through thin bridges of points and can merge visibly separate groups; complete linkage forces compactness and splits elongated ones. I default to Ward on continuous, comparably scaled data because it produces balanced trees, and switch to average linkage when I only have a precomputed distance matrix.

interview.question: Why might you prefer hierarchical clustering over a flat method on the same dataset?
interview.answer: Two reasons. First, you get every granularity from a single fit, so you can inspect two, five, and twenty clusters without refitting and pick the level that matches the decision you are making. Second, it works directly from a distance matrix, so it handles similarity measures like edit distance or Jaccard where computing a mean point is not defined.

interview.question: What is the main risk in interpreting a dendrogram?
interview.answer: Believing it reflects real structure. The algorithm produces a tree from any input, including pure noise, and its greedy merges are irreversible, so an early bad join is baked in permanently. Before reading a hierarchy into it, I would check that the merge heights show a clear jump somewhere and that the clusters survive on resampled data.

dbscan-and-density-based-clustering.text: DBSCAN defines a cluster as a region where points are packed closely enough together, and it grows clusters by reachability. You set two parameters: a radius, and a minimum number of neighbours a point needs within that radius to count as a core point. Core points that fall inside each other's radius chain together, dragging along the ordinary points on their fringes, and whatever is left over is labelled noise. Because clusters spread along wherever the density goes, they can be long, curved, or ring-shaped, and the number of them is an output rather than an input.
dbscan-and-density-based-clustering.deep_text:
Suppose you are clustering GPS pings with the radius set to 50 metres and the minimum neighbour count set to 5. A ping with seven other pings inside 50 metres is a core point. Another core point 40 metres away is directly reachable from it, so they join the same cluster, and a third core point 40 metres beyond that joins too — even though the first and third are 80 metres apart, well outside the radius. That transitivity is the whole trick: density-reachability chains, so a cluster can trace a road for kilometres while never containing two points more than 50 metres apart. A ping with only two neighbours but sitting inside a core point's radius becomes a border point, joined to that cluster but unable to extend it further. A ping alone in a field is noise, and DBSCAN says so explicitly rather than forcing it into the nearest group. That explicit noise label is often the most valuable output, since it doubles as outlier detection.

The misconception is that DBSCAN is parameter-free because you do not specify a cluster count. You trade one parameter for two harder ones. The radius in particular is unforgiving: slightly too large and separate groups merge into one blob, slightly too small and a real cluster shatters into fragments plus a lot of noise. A common heuristic is to sort every point's distance to its k-th nearest neighbour, plot those distances, and pick the radius at the sharp rise in that curve. The deeper limitation follows from having a single global radius: if one region of your data is dense and another is sparse but real, no single value works for both, and the sparse cluster gets classified as noise. Variants such as OPTICS and HDBSCAN exist precisely to handle varying density.

Reach for DBSCAN when clusters have irregular shapes, when you genuinely do not know how many there are, and when some points should legitimately belong to nothing — spatial data, sensor traces, fraud screening. Avoid it when densities vary widely across your data, and be careful in high dimensions, where distances concentrate so tightly that a meaningful radius stops existing at all.

interview.question: Why does DBSCAN find non-convex clusters when centroid methods can't?
interview.answer: Because membership is defined by chained reachability rather than distance to a single representative point. Two points at opposite ends of a long curved cluster can be far apart yet connected through a chain of overlapping dense neighbourhoods. A method that assigns points to the nearest centre has no such mechanism, so its boundaries are always straight cuts between centres.

interview.question: How do you actually choose the radius parameter?
interview.answer: The usual approach is a k-distance plot: for the chosen minimum-neighbour value k, compute each point's distance to its k-th nearest neighbour, sort those descending, and look for the knee where distances rise sharply. That knee marks where points stop being in dense regions. I treat the result as a starting point and sanity-check the noise fraction, since a run labelling 40% of the data as noise usually means the radius is too small.

interview.question: When is DBSCAN the wrong tool?
interview.answer: When density varies meaningfully across the dataset, because a single global radius cannot serve both a dense region and a sparse one — the sparse cluster gets dismissed as noise. It also degrades badly in high dimensions where distances concentrate and every point has roughly the same neighbour distance. In those cases I would reduce dimensions first or use a variant like HDBSCAN that adapts to local density.

gaussian-mixture-models.text: A Gaussian mixture model treats the data as coming from several bell-shaped distributions blended together, and fits them by asking, for every point, the probability that each component produced it. Nothing is assigned outright. A point sitting between two components might be 70% one and 30% the other, and those fractional responsibilities are what get used to update each component's mean, its covariance, and its overall weight. Because each component carries a full covariance matrix, it can be stretched, tilted, and sized independently, which lets the model fit elongated and overlapping groups.
gaussian-mixture-models.deep_text:
Fitting uses expectation-maximisation, which alternates in the same spirit as any assign-then-update scheme but with soft numbers. In the E step you compute each point's responsibility under each component from its current mean, covariance, and mixing weight. In the M step you recompute each component's parameters as a weighted average over all points, using those responsibilities as the weights. Take a two-component fit to customer session lengths where component one is centred at 3 minutes with a tight spread and component two at 25 minutes with a wide one. A 9-minute session might come out 0.6 responsibility to the first and 0.4 to the second, so it contributes 0.6 of a point to the first component's new mean and 0.4 to the second's. Each iteration cannot decrease the likelihood of the data, so it converges — to a local optimum, dependent on initialisation, which is why implementations typically seed from a quick hard-assignment run.

The misconception is that soft assignment means calibrated confidence. Those responsibilities are probabilities under the assumption that the data really is a mixture of Gaussians. If the true shape is skewed, heavy-tailed, or bounded at zero, the model will still report a confident-looking 0.85 that means very little. Related trap: with unconstrained covariance, a component can collapse onto a single point, shrinking its variance toward zero and driving the likelihood to infinity. Regularisation on the covariance, or tying covariances across components, is what prevents that degenerate solution.

The practical payoff over hard assignment is twofold. First, overlap is represented honestly — you can flag boundary points instead of pretending a coin flip was a decision. Second, because a mixture is a proper probability model, you can score a brand-new point's likelihood under it, which turns the fitted model into a density estimate and a natural anomaly detector, and you can use likelihood-based criteria to compare fits with different component counts. Reach for it when groups overlap, differ in spread or orientation, and you need probabilities downstream. Avoid it when features are far from Gaussian even after transformation, when dimensionality is high relative to sample size — a full covariance matrix has quadratically many parameters to estimate — or when you simply need fast, hard labels on a very large dataset.

interview.question: What does a Gaussian mixture give you that a hard-assignment clustering doesn't?
interview.answer: Two things. Soft responsibilities, so overlapping regions are represented as genuine uncertainty rather than forced into one group, which lets you route boundary cases to review instead of acting on a coin flip. And a full probability model over the feature space, so you can score the likelihood of a new unseen point — useful for anomaly detection and for comparing fits with different component counts using likelihood-based criteria.

interview.question: Why would you constrain the covariance matrices, and what happens if you don't?
interview.answer: With unconstrained full covariances, a component can collapse onto a single data point: its variance shrinks toward zero and the likelihood shoots to infinity, which is a degenerate solution rather than a fit. Adding a small regularisation term to the diagonal, or tying or restricting covariances across components, prevents that. Constraints also help when you have far fewer samples than a full covariance matrix has parameters to estimate.

interview.question: Your responsibilities look confident but the clusters seem wrong. What is your hypothesis?
interview.answer: That the Gaussian assumption is violated. The responsibilities are probabilities conditional on the data actually being a mixture of Gaussians, so on skewed, heavy-tailed, or bounded features the model will still produce sharp-looking numbers that mean nothing. I would check the marginal distributions, try a transform such as a log on positive skewed features, and compare against a method that makes no distributional assumption.

dimensionality-reduction-and-representat.text: A record with 800 raw columns is rarely 800 independent facts about that record. Most of those columns are correlated, noisy, or nearly constant, and the useful information often lives in a much smaller number of underlying factors. Finding those factors serves two quite different goals that people constantly confuse: producing a picture a human can look at, and producing a feature vector a machine can compute on. The methods here split along that line, and along whether the transformation is fixed by geometry or learned from data.
dimensionality-reduction-and-representat.deep_text:
Start with why the problem exists at all. High-dimensional spaces behave counterintuitively — distances concentrate, neighbourhoods stop being local, and models need vastly more data to cover the space — and that motivation node also sets out what you are trading away, since every reduction discards something. It comes first because the rest of the section is a set of answers to a question you have to feel before the answers mean anything.

The remaining three divide by purpose. t-SNE and UMAP exist to make two-dimensional pictures. They deliberately distort global structure to preserve local neighbourhoods, which makes them excellent for spotting groups by eye and dangerous as inputs to anything downstream. Autoencoders sit at the other end: a network learns to squeeze data through a narrow layer and rebuild it, so the bottleneck becomes a compressed code shaped by whatever nonlinear structure the data actually has. That code is meant to be used, not looked at. Embeddings then generalise the idea one step further — any dense vector where geometric closeness encodes semantic similarity, however it was produced, including as a by-product of training a model on some other task entirely.

Read in that order, the section moves from motivation, to visualisation, to learned compression, to the general notion of a representation. Note that the classical linear workhorse, principal component analysis, is covered separately under training and optimisation; several methods here are routinely run on top of its output rather than on raw features, so the two sections are meant to be used together.

why-reduce-dimensions.text: Adding features feels free and is not. As dimensions grow, the volume of the space explodes, your data becomes a sparse scattering in a mostly empty box, and the distances that clustering and nearest-neighbour methods depend on start collapsing toward each other until nothing looks meaningfully closer than anything else. Models need more data to fill the space, training and storage costs climb, and correlated columns add variance without adding information. Reducing dimensions trades a little fidelity for denser coverage, faster computation, and features that downstream algorithms can actually use.
why-reduce-dimensions.deep_text:
Make the sparsity concrete. Split each feature into ten bins. With one feature you have ten cells, and a thousand samples give you a hundred per cell — plenty. With five features you have 100,000 cells and a thousand samples cover 1% of them. With ten features you have ten billion cells, and essentially every sample sits alone in its own cell with empty space in every direction. Nothing about the data changed; the space around it grew. This is why a nearest-neighbour classifier that works beautifully on five features degrades on fifty: the nearest neighbour is no longer near in any meaningful sense. The same effect breaks distance-based clustering, because the ratio between the farthest and nearest point from any given query drifts toward one, so every point looks about equally far from every other.

The misconception is that this is purely about compute — that reduction is an optimisation you apply when training gets slow. Statistical cost is the bigger issue. Every extra column is another parameter to estimate from the same fixed number of rows, so variance rises and the model fits noise that happens to correlate with the target in your sample. A model with more features than rows can fit the training set perfectly and learn nothing. Reduction is a form of regularisation as much as a speedup, which is why it can improve held-out accuracy rather than merely preserving it.

The saving grace is that real data rarely fills its nominal space. Pixels in photographs, sensor readings from one machine, and survey responses are all heavily correlated, so the data concentrates near a lower-dimensional surface inside the big space. Reduction is the attempt to find coordinates on that surface. The decision rule: reduce when features are many and correlated, when a distance-based method is involved, or when samples are few relative to columns. Do not reduce reflexively — with abundant data and a model that handles high dimensions natively, such as a regularised linear model or a gradient-boosted tree, you may be throwing away signal for nothing. Also distinguish reduction from selection: selection keeps a subset of your original interpretable columns, while reduction builds new composite coordinates that are harder to explain to a stakeholder. Principal component analysis is the standard linear starting point and is covered under training and optimisation.

interview.question: Why do distance-based methods degrade in high dimensions?
interview.answer: As dimensions increase, the ratio between the farthest and nearest point from any query drifts toward one, so relative distances lose their discriminating power. Every point ends up roughly equidistant from every other, which undermines nearest-neighbour lookups, distance-based clustering, and any radius-based rule. The effect is worst when the extra dimensions are noisy, since each one contributes variance to the distance without contributing signal.

interview.question: When would you deliberately not reduce dimensions?
interview.answer: When I have plenty of rows relative to columns and I am using a model that handles high dimensions well, such as a regularised linear model or gradient-boosted trees, reduction mostly costs me signal and interpretability. I would also avoid it when stakeholders need to act on specific original features, since composite coordinates are much harder to explain than a subset of real columns.

interview.question: Is dimensionality reduction the same as feature selection?
interview.answer: No. Selection keeps a subset of the original columns, so the surviving features stay interpretable and you can drop the rest from your data pipeline entirely. Reduction constructs new coordinates as combinations of all the originals, which usually retains more information per output dimension but means you still need every input feature at inference time and the outputs no longer have names.

t-sne-and-umap-for-visualisation.text: t-SNE and UMAP squash high-dimensional data down to two or three dimensions specifically so a person can look at it. Both work by preserving neighbourhoods: they measure which points are close in the original space, then arrange points on the plane so that those same neighbours stay close, letting everything else fall where it may. The result is a scatter plot where visible blobs usually correspond to real groups. What they do not preserve is global geometry, so the distance between two blobs on the picture is not a quantity you can trust.
t-sne-and-umap-for-visualisation.deep_text:
The mechanism is worth knowing because it explains the failure modes. t-SNE converts distances into neighbour probabilities in the original space, does the same in the two-dimensional layout using a heavy-tailed distribution, and then moves the points to make those two sets of probabilities match. UMAP builds a weighted neighbour graph instead and optimises a low-dimensional layout to match its connectivity; it is generally faster and holds onto somewhat more of the large-scale arrangement, but the core trade is identical. Both have a knob controlling how many neighbours count as local — perplexity in t-SNE, n_neighbors in UMAP — and it changes the picture substantially. Run t-SNE on 20,000 handwritten digit images at perplexity 5 and you may get dozens of small fragments; at perplexity 50 you get roughly ten clean islands, with the ones for 4, 7, and 9 sitting near each other because those digits genuinely look alike. Neither picture is wrong; they are answers to different questions about scale.

The misconception, and it causes real damage in reviews, is reading the plot as a map. Cluster sizes are meaningless — the algorithms expand sparse regions and compress dense ones, so a visually large blob may hold fewer points than a small one. The gap between two clusters is meaningless too. And because both methods are stochastic and initialisation-dependent, two runs with different seeds produce different-looking layouts of the same data. Most damaging of all is feeding the two-dimensional coordinates into a downstream classifier or clustering algorithm as features. That output was optimised for a picture, discards global structure by design, and in t-SNE's case has no principled way to place a new point at all without refitting.

Use them for exploration: checking whether labelled classes separate at all, spotting a batch effect where samples cluster by collection date rather than biology, eyeballing whether a learned representation has structure. Standard practice is to reduce to perhaps 30 or 50 dimensions with a linear method such as principal component analysis first, both for speed and to strip noise, then run t-SNE or UMAP on that. Vary the neighbour parameter and the seed, and only believe structure that survives. If you need coordinates that anything other than a human eye will consume, use a method built for that instead.

interview.question: Why shouldn't you use t-SNE output as features for a downstream model?
interview.answer: The embedding is optimised to preserve local neighbourhoods for visual inspection and explicitly sacrifices global geometry, so distances and directions in the plot do not correspond to anything a model can use. It is also stochastic, so the coordinates change between runs, and t-SNE has no natural way to project a new unseen point without refitting the whole thing. If I need learned coordinates for a model, I would use a method with a reusable transform.

interview.question: Two clusters appear far apart in a UMAP plot. What can you conclude?
interview.answer: Very little about how different they actually are. Both methods distort inter-cluster distances to make the local structure fit on a plane, so a large gap is not evidence of large dissimilarity, and cluster areas do not reflect point counts either. What I can reasonably conclude is that the points within each blob are neighbours in the original space, and I would verify any apparent separation with a measurement in the original feature space.

interview.question: How would you sanity-check a t-SNE or UMAP plot before showing it in a review?
interview.answer: Rerun it at several values of the neighbourhood parameter and several random seeds, and only present structure that survives all of them. I would also colour the points by metadata I did not use — collection date, source system, batch — to catch the case where the visible groups are an artefact of how the data was gathered rather than anything about the subject.

autoencoders-as-learned-compression.text: An autoencoder is a network trained to copy its input to its output through a deliberately narrow middle layer. The encoder squeezes the input down to a small vector, the decoder tries to rebuild the original from just that vector, and the training signal is how badly the reconstruction misses. Nothing but the data itself supervises this, yet the bottleneck forces the network to discard whatever is redundant and keep whatever is needed to reconstruct. The compressed vector at the middle becomes a learned representation, shaped by nonlinear structure a fixed linear projection cannot capture.
autoencoders-as-learned-compression.deep_text:
Picture 28-by-28 greyscale images, 784 numbers each. The encoder maps 784 down through a few layers to a 32-number code; the decoder maps 32 back up to 784; the loss is mean squared error between input and output pixels. After training, feeding an image through the encoder gives you 32 numbers that stand in for it. Reconstructions come back slightly blurred, which tells you precisely what was thrown away: fine, high-frequency detail that costs many parameters and carries little of what distinguishes one image from another. Shrink the bottleneck to 2 and reconstructions become unusable mush; widen it to 700 and the reconstructions are near perfect but the network has learned little, since it barely had to compress. The bottleneck width is the compression ratio, and it is the main design decision.

The misconception is that low reconstruction error means a good representation. It does not. Given enough capacity and no constraint, a network can learn something close to an identity mapping that copies inputs through without extracting anything useful, scoring beautifully on the loss and producing a code no downstream task benefits from. This is why variants exist that add pressure beyond the bottleneck. A denoising autoencoder corrupts the input — masking pixels, adding noise — and asks the network to reconstruct the clean original, which forces it to model how features relate rather than memorise them. A sparse autoencoder penalises how many code units activate at once. A variational autoencoder constrains the code to follow a distribution, which makes the space continuous enough to sample from and generate new examples.

The useful comparison is against a linear projection. Principal component analysis, covered elsewhere, finds the best linear subspace, and a single-hidden-layer autoencoder with linear activations recovers essentially that same subspace. The gain from an autoencoder comes entirely from nonlinearity and depth: it can follow a curved surface that no linear projection can. The costs are real too — you need enough data to train a network, the learned dimensions have no interpretation or ordering by importance, and results depend on architecture and initialisation. Reach for one when the data is large, plentiful, and plausibly nonlinear, or when you need a learned encoder that also serves as an anomaly detector, since inputs unlike anything in training reconstruct poorly and that error is a usable score. Skip it when a linear method already explains most of the variance.

interview.question: Why does the bottleneck matter, and what happens if you make it too wide?
interview.answer: The bottleneck is the only thing forcing the network to compress; without it there is a trivial solution where the network copies its input straight through. A wide bottleneck approaches that trivial solution — reconstruction error looks excellent while the code has learned almost nothing generalisable. That is why low reconstruction loss on its own is not evidence of a useful representation.

interview.question: When would an autoencoder beat a linear projection, and when would it not?
interview.answer: It wins when the data lies on a curved surface rather than a flat subspace, and when you have enough data to fit a network without overfitting. It loses when a linear method already captures most of the variance, because you then pay training cost and lose interpretability for nothing, and when data is scarce. Linear components also come ordered by importance, which autoencoder code units do not.

interview.question: How would you use an autoencoder for anomaly detection?
interview.answer: Train it on data you believe is normal, then score new inputs by their reconstruction error. Inputs resembling the training distribution rebuild accurately; genuinely unusual ones do not, so the error becomes an anomaly score you threshold. The main caveat is that a high-capacity network can generalise well enough to reconstruct anomalies too, so I would keep the bottleneck tight and validate the threshold on known bad examples.

embeddings-as-dense-representations.text: An embedding is a fixed-length vector of real numbers that stands in for something — a user, a product, a word, an image — arranged so that geometric closeness means semantic similarity. Instead of a 100,000-column one-hot vector where every item is equally distant from every other, you get maybe 128 numbers where related items land near each other. The vectors are learned, usually as a by-product of training a model to predict something, and once learned they transfer: the same product vectors can feed a recommender, a search ranker, and a churn model.
embeddings-as-dense-representations.deep_text:
The contrast with one-hot encoding is the whole point. Represent 50,000 products as one-hot and every pair is exactly the same distance apart, so the encoding carries no information about the items themselves — a model must learn each product's behaviour from scratch, and rare products, which are most of them, never get enough examples. Train an embedding table of 50,000 by 64 as part of a model predicting which products get bought together, and the parameters adjust so that products appearing in similar contexts drift toward similar vectors. Afterwards, the nearest neighbours of a running shoe are other running shoes, and a product with only forty purchase events inherits useful geometry from the products it co-occurs with. The general recipe holds well beyond products: initialise a lookup table of vectors randomly, train it end-to-end on any task where the items appear, and keep the table.

A useful concrete check is cosine similarity between two vectors — the cosine of the angle between them, which ignores magnitude and measures direction. Two documents about the same subject score perhaps 0.85; unrelated ones score near zero. This is what powers similarity search: encode the query, find the nearest vectors, return those items. That in turn is why approximate nearest-neighbour indexes and vector databases exist, since scanning 50 million vectors per query is not viable.

The misconception worth stating plainly is that embeddings are universal or objective. They are not. A vector space inherits the objective it was trained on, so product vectors learned from co-purchase encode substitutability and complementarity, while vectors learned from text descriptions encode topical similarity, and the two will disagree about which items are alike. Neither is wrong; they answer different questions. Embeddings also inherit whatever biases and staleness sit in their training data, and they drift — a table trained on last year's catalogue quietly degrades as new items appear with no vector at all, the cold-start problem. Reach for embeddings when cardinality is high, when items have meaningful similarity relationships, or when you want one representation serving several downstream tasks. Skip them for low-cardinality categoricals, where one-hot is simpler and more interpretable, and be wary when you cannot explain what similarity your particular vector space actually encodes.

interview.question: Why use an embedding instead of one-hot encoding a high-cardinality categorical?
interview.answer: One-hot makes every category equidistant, so the model learns each category independently and rare ones never accumulate enough examples to learn from. An embedding places similar categories near each other in a dense space, letting statistical strength flow between them, and it reduces a 50,000-column input to a few dozen numbers. The trade is interpretability: you can no longer point at a column and name it.

interview.question: Two embedding spaces disagree about which items are similar. How is that possible?
interview.answer: Because each space encodes the objective it was trained on. Vectors learned from co-purchase behaviour capture substitutes and complements; vectors learned from item descriptions capture topical similarity. Both are internally consistent and neither is the true similarity, so before using a space I want to know what task produced it and whether that notion of similarity matches the decision I am making.

interview.question: What operational problems do embeddings introduce in production?
interview.answer: Cold start, drift, and retrieval cost. New items have no vector until the table is retrained, so you need a fallback such as encoding from content features. The space also shifts each time you retrain, which means anything cached — precomputed neighbours, downstream models consuming the vectors — has to be rebuilt in step. And similarity search over millions of vectors needs an approximate nearest-neighbour index, which brings its own accuracy-versus-latency tuning.

learning-with-limited-labels.text: Labels are the expensive part of most machine learning projects. Annotating a hundred thousand medical images or fraud cases costs expert time you probably do not have, while the unlabelled data piles up for free. Four strategies attack that gap from different directions: model what normal looks like so you never need labelled failures, invent a training task the data labels itself, borrow a model someone else already trained and adapt it, or spend your tiny annotation budget on the examples that teach the model most. They combine well, and a real project usually uses several.
learning-with-limited-labels.deep_text:
The four children are ordered by how much labelling they assume. Anomaly and outlier detection sits first because it often needs no labels at all: you characterise the normal majority and flag whatever does not fit, which is exactly the right framing when the interesting class is rare and its failure modes are not known in advance. Self-supervised pretext tasks come next. Instead of avoiding supervision, they manufacture it — hide part of the input and predict it from the rest — so the labels come free from the data's own structure, and the model ends up with a representation that captures how the data is put together.

Transfer learning and fine-tuning follows naturally, because it is what you do with such a pretrained model, or with any model trained on a related large dataset: keep the learned features and adapt the last part to your specific task with a small labelled set. The dependency runs one way, which is why self-supervision comes first — pretraining produces the thing transfer learning consumes.

Active learning comes last because it assumes you have a working model and a labelling budget, and asks a different question: not how to avoid labels, but which labels to buy. Feeding your annotator the examples the current model is least sure about typically reaches a target accuracy with a fraction of the annotations that random sampling needs.

Across all four, the recurring idea is that unlabelled data carries real information about the structure of your problem, and the labels only have to pin that structure to the specific outcome you care about.

anomaly-and-outlier-detection.text: Anomaly detection flips the usual setup: instead of learning to separate two labelled classes, you build a model of what normal looks like and flag whatever fails to fit. That framing suits problems where the interesting events are rare, varied, and not fully known in advance — equipment failures, fraud, intrusions. You cannot enumerate every way a machine can break, but you can characterise thousands of hours of it working. The output is typically a continuous score of how unusual something is, and where you put the threshold on that score is a business decision, not a statistical one.
anomaly-and-outlier-detection.deep_text:
The methods form a few families. Statistical approaches fit a distribution and flag low-probability points, which works when the data is well behaved and interpretable thresholds matter. Distance and density approaches flag points far from their neighbours or in sparse regions; local outlier factor compares a point's local density to its neighbours', catching points that are unusual relative to their own region even when the global density varies. Isolation forests take a different angle entirely, randomly splitting the feature space and noting that anomalies get isolated in fewer splits because they sit in sparse regions, which makes them fast and effective in moderate dimensions. Reconstruction approaches train a model to rebuild normal data and score by how badly it fails on new input.

A worked case shows why thresholds dominate. Suppose you score a million daily card transactions and set a threshold flagging 0.1% of them, so a thousand alerts a day. If genuine fraud runs at roughly one in ten thousand transactions, there are about a hundred real cases in that million. Even if your detector catches eighty of them, your thousand alerts are 92% false positives — and a fraud team that can review two hundred cases a day is now drowning. Tightening the threshold to a hundred alerts might keep forty of the eighty, halving recall to double precision. That trade, not the choice of algorithm, is what determines whether the system is usable.

The misconception is that anomaly and rare-class classification are the same problem. They are not. If you have a decent number of labelled positives and the failure modes are stable, a supervised classifier with class weighting will almost always beat an unsupervised detector, because it learns what makes a positive positive rather than merely what makes it unusual. Unsupervised detection earns its place when positives are near-nonexistent, when novel failure modes matter more than known ones, or when labels arrive too late to train on. A second trap: if your training data already contains undetected anomalies, the model learns them as normal and stops flagging them. In production, add drift monitoring, since a rising alert rate usually means the world changed rather than that attacks spiked, and always route alerts through a feedback loop so confirmed cases eventually become labels you can supervise on.

interview.question: When would you use a supervised classifier instead of an unsupervised anomaly detector?
interview.answer: Whenever I have a reasonable number of confirmed positive examples and the failure modes are reasonably stable. A classifier learns what distinguishes a positive, which is strictly more informative than learning what is merely unusual, and class weighting or resampling handles the imbalance. I reserve unsupervised detection for cases where positives are near-nonexistent, arrive too late to train on, or where the novel failure modes are the ones that matter.

interview.question: How do you set the threshold on an anomaly score?
interview.answer: From the downstream capacity and cost, not from the score distribution. If a review team can handle two hundred cases a day, that caps the alert volume and the threshold follows. I would then quantify what that volume buys in recall on whatever confirmed positives exist, and present the precision-recall trade explicitly rather than picking a percentile and calling it done.

interview.question: What goes wrong when you train an anomaly detector on historical production data?
interview.answer: The history almost certainly contains undetected anomalies, and the model absorbs them as normal, so exactly the failures that already slipped past you keep slipping past. It is also fitted to a past distribution, so as normal behaviour drifts the alert rate climbs for reasons unrelated to real anomalies. I would monitor the alert rate as a first-class metric and periodically refit on data cleaned with whatever confirmed labels have accumulated.

self-supervised-pretext-tasks.text: Self-supervision manufactures labels out of the data's own structure. You define a task where the answer is already contained in the input — hide some of it, then train the model to predict what you hid. Mask words in a sentence and predict them. Cut an image into patches and predict their arrangement. Distort an image two ways and train the model to recognise both versions as the same thing. Nobody annotates anything, yet solving these puzzles forces the model to learn how the data is put together, and that understanding transfers to tasks you actually care about.
self-supervised-pretext-tasks.deep_text:
The task you train on is called the pretext task, and it is deliberately disposable. Nobody needs a system that predicts which of four rotations was applied to a photograph. The point is that a model cannot do it reliably without having learned what objects look like and which way up they normally sit. Concretely: take ten million unlabelled product photos, rotate each by 0, 90, 180, or 270 degrees at random, and train a network to classify the rotation. The label came free from the rotation you chose. After training, throw away the four-way output layer and keep the encoder, whose intermediate features now respond to shapes, textures, and object parts. Masked prediction works the same way in text — hide 15% of tokens and predict them from context, the recipe behind models like BERT — and contrastive methods pull two augmented views of one example together while pushing different examples apart.

Designing the pretext task is the real skill, because there are always shortcuts. A famous class of failures: models asked to predict the relative position of two image patches learned to match up sensor noise and compression artefacts along the shared edge, solving the puzzle perfectly while learning nothing about content. The remedy is to make the shortcut unavailable — leave gaps between patches, jitter colours, randomise compression. Similarly, in contrastive learning, if your augmentations are too weak the model can identify matching views from colour histograms alone; too strong and the two views no longer share the content you wanted it to learn.

The misconception is that self-supervision is unsupervised learning under a new name. The mechanism is ordinary supervised training with gradients and a loss; the only difference is where the labels come from. That distinction matters practically, because everything you know about supervised training still applies, and because the pretext task's own accuracy is not the metric that counts. Evaluate the representation on the downstream task you care about, typically by freezing the encoder and fitting a simple classifier on a small labelled set. Reach for this when unlabelled data is abundant and labels are scarce or expensive. Skip it when you have only modest data, when a suitable pretrained model already exists for your domain, or when the labelled set is large enough to train directly — pretraining costs real compute, and it pays off in the label-scarce regime, not everywhere.

interview.question: Is self-supervised learning just unsupervised learning?
interview.answer: No. The training loop is ordinary supervised learning with a loss and gradients; what is unusual is that the labels are derived automatically from the input rather than annotated by a person. That framing matters because it means the usual supervised concerns — leakage, shortcuts, overfitting to the pretext task — all still apply.

interview.question: How do you know a pretext task is teaching the model something useful?
interview.answer: Not from its own accuracy, which can be high for the wrong reasons. The standard evaluation is to freeze the pretrained encoder, fit a simple linear classifier on top using a small labelled set from the real task, and compare against the same classifier trained on raw features or a randomly initialised encoder. If the gap is small, the pretext task probably admitted a shortcut.

interview.question: What is a shortcut in this context and how do you prevent one?
interview.answer: A shortcut is any low-level cue that solves the pretext task without requiring semantic understanding — matching compression artefacts along a shared patch edge, or identifying augmented views by their colour histogram. Prevention means removing the cue by construction: introduce gaps between patches, randomise colour and compression, and generally check by hand whether a trivial statistic could solve your puzzle.

transfer-learning-and-fine-tuning.text: Transfer learning starts from a model already trained on a large dataset and adapts it to your smaller problem instead of training from scratch. The premise is that the early layers learn general structure — edges and textures in vision, syntax and word relations in text — that is useful far beyond the original task, while only the last layers are specific to it. So you keep the learned weights, replace the output head with one shaped for your labels, and train. With a few thousand examples this routinely beats anything you could train from random initialisation.
transfer-learning-and-fine-tuning.deep_text:
There is a spectrum of how much you change, and picking a point on it is the main decision. At one end, feature extraction: freeze the whole pretrained network, run your data through it once, and fit a small classifier on the resulting vectors. Fast, cheap, hard to overfit, and the right choice when you have a few hundred labels. At the other end, full fine-tuning: unfreeze everything and train the entire network on your data at a low learning rate. Most expressive, most data-hungry, most likely to overfit. In between, unfreeze only the last block or two, which is where the task-specific representations live.

A concrete case: 2,000 photographs of manufacturing defects across five categories. Training a network from scratch on 2,000 images gives you something that memorises the training set and fails on new photos. Starting from a network pretrained on a large general image corpus and training only a new five-way head gets you a usable model in minutes. Then unfreezing the final convolutional block at a learning rate perhaps ten to a hundred times lower than usual typically adds a few more points, because those layers can adjust to the specific textures of metal and plastic that the general corpus underrepresents. Use a low rate deliberately: a high one on a pretrained network destroys the features you came for, an effect called catastrophic forgetting, where the first few large gradient steps overwrite good weights before the model has learned anything to replace them with.

The misconception is that more pretraining data always transfers better. What matters is the relationship between source and target domains. A network pretrained on everyday photographs transfers well to product images and poorly to spectrograms or medical scans, which look nothing like natural scenes; in a genuinely distant domain the early layers may be no better than random and full fine-tuning becomes necessary, or the transfer fails outright. Check the domain gap before assuming a benefit.

The decision rule follows the same two variables: how much labelled data you have, and how far your domain sits from the source. Little data and a close domain, freeze and train a head. Lots of data and a distant domain, fine-tune everything. In between, unfreeze progressively and watch validation loss, since the overfitting signal shows up early. Also inherit the source's preprocessing exactly — the same input size and normalisation statistics — because a mismatch there quietly costs more accuracy than any of these choices.

interview.question: How do you decide how many layers to unfreeze?
interview.answer: It comes down to labelled data volume and domain distance. With a few hundred examples in a domain close to the pretraining data, I freeze everything and train only a new head, since anything more will overfit. With tens of thousands of examples or a domain far from the source, I unfreeze progressively from the top and watch validation loss, stopping when it stops improving or starts to diverge from training loss.

interview.question: Why use a much lower learning rate when fine-tuning?
interview.answer: The pretrained weights are already in a good region of the space, and large gradient steps early in fine-tuning overwrite them before the model has learned anything better — catastrophic forgetting. A low rate, often one to two orders of magnitude below what you would use from scratch, lets the network adapt while preserving the features you started for. Warming up the new head first with the base frozen also helps, since a randomly initialised head produces large initial gradients.

interview.question: When does transfer learning fail to help?
interview.answer: When the source and target domains are genuinely dissimilar — a network pretrained on natural photographs gives you little on spectrograms or certain medical imaging, because even the low-level filters do not match. It also stops mattering when your own labelled dataset is large enough to train from scratch effectively. And a subtle failure is preprocessing mismatch: different input resolution or normalisation statistics than the source used will silently degrade results regardless of how you freeze layers.

active-learning.text: When annotation costs real money or expert time, the examples you choose to label matter as much as how many. Active learning makes the model pick them. Train on whatever small labelled set you have, run the model over the unlabelled pool, and send a human only the examples the model is least confident about — the ones near its decision boundary, where a label resolves genuine ambiguity. Retrain, repeat. Because random sampling wastes most of its budget on easy examples the model already handles, this loop often reaches target accuracy on a fraction of the labels.
active-learning.deep_text:
Uncertainty sampling is the standard selection rule. For a classifier, rank unlabelled points by how close the predicted probability sits to the decision boundary, or by the margin between the top two classes, or by entropy across all classes. An alternative family, query-by-committee, trains several models and picks the points they disagree about most, which captures a different kind of uncertainty — disagreement about the model rather than about the point.

A realistic loop: 200,000 unlabelled support tickets, an annotator who can do 500 a day, and a target of a usable seven-way classifier. Label 500 at random for a seed model. Score the remaining 199,500, take the 500 with the highest prediction entropy, label those, retrain. After ten rounds you have 5,000 labels chosen mostly from confusing, boundary-straddling tickets rather than the flood of obvious billing questions. The typical shape of the result is that active selection reaches accuracy that random sampling would need several times as many labels to match — with the caveat that the gain shrinks as the labelled set grows, since eventually most remaining uncertainty is irreducible noise rather than missing information.

The misconception is that the most uncertain example is always the most valuable. It frequently is not. Genuinely ambiguous, corrupted, or mislabelled items sit at maximum uncertainty forever and teach nothing, so a pure uncertainty rule can spend an entire budget on garbage. Practical systems combine uncertainty with a representativeness term, preferring uncertain points that also sit in dense regions of the pool, so each label speaks for many similar unlabelled items. Batching creates a related trap: the top 500 most uncertain points are often 500 near-duplicates of the same hard case, so you need a diversity constraint within the batch or you buy one insight five hundred times.

Practically, note that the labelled set is no longer a random sample of your data, so held-out accuracy measured on it is biased and you need a separate randomly sampled test set kept out of the loop entirely. Reach for active learning when the unlabelled pool is large, annotation is genuinely expensive, and retraining is cheap enough to run repeatedly. Skip it when labelling is cheap, when the pool is small enough to annotate fully, or when each retraining round takes days — the coordination overhead of a human-in-the-loop cycle then outweighs the labels you save.

interview.question: Why isn't picking the single most uncertain example always the right move?
interview.answer: Because maximum uncertainty often marks noise rather than information — corrupted records, genuinely ambiguous cases, or mislabelled data that stays uncertain no matter how much you label around it. A pure uncertainty rule can burn an entire budget there. Combining uncertainty with a representativeness term, so the chosen point also sits in a dense region of the pool, makes each label count for many similar items.

interview.question: What breaks when you select a whole batch by uncertainty rather than one point at a time?
interview.answer: The top-scoring points tend to be near-duplicates of each other, all reflecting the same hard case, so you pay for hundreds of labels and learn one thing. Real batch active learning adds a diversity constraint — clustering the candidates and sampling across clusters, or a submodular selection criterion — so the batch covers distinct regions of uncertainty.

interview.question: How do you evaluate a model trained through an active learning loop?
interview.answer: On a separate test set sampled randomly and held out of the loop from the start. The actively labelled set is deliberately biased toward hard, boundary-straddling examples, so measuring on it understates real-world accuracy and gives you no usable estimate of production performance. I would fix that random test set before the first round and never let the selection process touch it.
